title: Hidden-thinking scorer reads 0 on all 2,086 llama-server traces with recorded reasoning (2,002 above 10 s): the gate's silent-thinking rule cannot see them
description:
Finding: boar-bench's hidden-thinking scorer reads exactly 0 on every llama-server trace where the adapter itself recorded hidden reasoning, so the gate rule written to catch silent thinking cannot see it on that backend.

Full report with tables, code quotes and scripts: https://files.catbox.moe/ocrc14.txt

Measured on all 1,062 public trace files (45,062 traces, hashes checked against TRACES.tsv; dataset r4topunk/boar-traces at f96e277cf8584b38c35c01106c1fe77457dfaa81; code r4topunk/boar-bench at b41a25acfabf89f1d015103ca1329554f985a257):
- 2,086 llama-server traces (all Qwen, 26 run folders) have timing.reasoningMs above 1 s. The scorer's hidden_think_ms is 0.0 in 2,086 of 2,086.
- 2,002 of them are above 10 s, the gate threshold. qwen3-4b-thinking: adapter p50 12.6 s vs scorer p50 0.0 s. Deep tier (1,853 traces): adapter p50 52.9 s vs 0.0 s.
- Control: the 100 node-backend Gemma traces with reasoning are detected 100 of 100 (scorer p50 11.4 s vs adapter 11.3 s).
- The llama-server backend produced 28,737 of the 45,062 public traces.

Cause, traced in the code:
1. scorers/timing.py:24-42 computes hidden_think_ms as first visible token event minus first token event. It is above 0 only if blank token events precede the text.
2. On the llama-server backend reasoning never becomes an event. adapters/desktop-node/runner/server.ts:107-108: "Visible text goes to onText; reasoning never does." Lines 123-126 only set firstReasoningMs and count tokens. In the data: 0 of 2,086 traces have a blank token before the first visible one.
3. The adapter writes the real value to timing.reasoningMs, firstVisibleMs and reasoningTokens (adapter.ts:986-997; protocol index.ts:127-131). No .py file in the repo reads any of the three.
4. The author's own spec (boar-research, rnd/research/anvil/specs/adapter-llama-server-backend.md:63) calls those fields "the harness TTFT fix the coordinator assigned on 2026-10-02". The adapter half shipped; the harness half did not.

What it breaks:
- harness/gate.py:16-20, 45-46, 59-67: rule empty-or-silent (b) fails a candidate with hidden thinking above 10 s where the base had none; its header names the purpose: "Anvil's thinking-model failure: empty answers after ~19 s of invisible tokens." With the value at 0, a llama-server candidate that thinks silently for 19 s or 90 s passes (b). The rule's test (harness/tests/test_gate.py:163-173) builds its case from a blank token event, a shape this backend does not produce for reasoning, so the test passes while the rule is blind.
- harness/report.py:39-55, 155, 232-233: the hidden-thinking row has p50 0 and the warning flag stays off.
- harness/diff.py:37, 125 compares zeros.

Reproduce (scripts only read JSONL and transcribe the scorer; no repo code is run):
- Three files, 2 MB: python3 -I repro.py rnd/heldout/bench-v02/runs-think4b/t4-ZV-v02-s42.traces.jsonl rnd/heldout/vitalik-para1/runs-think4b/t4-Z-vpara-s42.traces.jsonl rnd/research/coordinator/arms/g4eng/runs/g4eng-v01-s44.traces.jsonl -> 0 on 89 of 89 and 51 of 51 (Qwen); Gemma control 0 on 0 of 50. Script: https://files.catbox.moe/f8thtn.py Output: https://files.catbox.moe/p72ec9.txt
- Whole dataset: python3 -I count_all.py /path/to/boar-traces. Script: https://files.catbox.moe/vr0fcd.py Output: https://files.catbox.moe/f6rbr6.txt

Fix (a few lines): in visible_timing use timing.reasoningMs as hidden_think_ms when it is a number, keep the event computation as fallback; add a gate test with reasoningMs above 10 s and no blank token events.

Limits, stated plainly: this affects the latency instruments (report, gate rule (b), diff), not the quality scores or the ratios of the article. The author reported the thinking cost of the think4b arm by hand in THINK4B.md ("ttft 19.9 s"), and those conclusions stand. ttft_visible_ms is correct on these traces. It was not established whether any gate decision in the record would have changed; that needs the pairs the author actually gated. Checked against the 31 earlier claims on this bounty: none concerns the timing scorer or these fields, and this does not derive from another claim.

title: Follow-up retrieval fails on the final build's own headline traces: 5 of 12 follow-up turns retrieve nothing on-topic, and one wrong answer carries a false citation
description:
The record closed follow-up retrieval in U5 ("no fix proposed... [the maintainer's FollowUp] rule already resolves the case"). The final build's own DEVICE-FINAL M1 traces contradict that verdict.

On M1 seed 42, 5 of the 12 non-health follow-up turns retrieved no on-topic passage on EITHER path: phone and desktop kept byte-identical garbage (e.g. cw-033#t3 "ok what's it good for besides being dry" kept the definition of the word "OK", a brownie recipe, and Peru cuisine; cw-034#t3 "which one is older" kept US-dollar advice and 401(k) limits; cx-036#t3 retrieved nothing at all). The kept bodies contain zero topic terms, yet the answers name the topic confidently: ungrounded answers from history/memory. Worst case: cw-034#t3 answers "The Alhambra is older than the Cordoba Mosque... [1]", inverted against its own rubric T3 (mosque begun 785-786, ~4.5 centuries before the Nasrid Alhambra), with "[1]" citing the US-dollars passage.

Mechanism, in the shipped FollowUp.kt: (1) the history-combined fallback fires only when the direct search returns an EMPTY list, but the retriever returns low-relevance matches instead of nothing, so the fallback is effectively dead; (2) the direct-path trigger matches pronouns only, missing "which one", "the second one", "my first question", and the 3-term fallback limit excludes long anaphoric questions, so they fall through with no history augmentation; (3) the published eval runner passes no history (DeviceEvalRunner.kt:365) while the shipped chat does (ChatViewModel.kt:683) -- with the caveat that the M1 build commit is not publicly verifiable, flagged in the analysis.

This does not change the headline U-total or phone/desktop parity (both paths fail identically; multi-turn items average 1.40/5 phone, 1.42/5 desktop). It reopens a closed verdict: U5 and QFORM tested the research engine and simulated the plan, never the final build's traces. Concrete fix specified in the analysis: relevance-gate the fallback, extend the triggers, anchor to the previous turn's kept articles (the record's own FOLLOWUP-r2 design), and retest on the M1 multi-turn items under the record's frozen gate (gold kept ON-OFF >= +5, 0 lost) plus a citation-support check. Record's own estimate: +0.02 to +0.05 U on reached follow-up items.

Full analysis with exact trace excerpts, file/line references, reproduction steps, and limitations: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Velixxyz/Velixxyz.github.io/main/poidh-1520/audit-followup-retrieval.md

Related prior claims, distinguished in the analysis: #9243 (same eval-runner file, different divergence: pack IDs/sort vs history), #9227 / #9503 / #9349 / #9251 (single-turn retrieval wall, not follow-ups), #9473 (delivery split, not follow-up mechanics), #9556 (citation stripping before judging, not false citations to users). No existing claim covers FollowUp, multi-turn retrieval, or anaphoric queries. Errata E1-E8 do not mention follow-up retrieval.

title: Deluin — The Wall on the Inside
description:
**In one breath:** Deluin builds walls, so when his parents opened Redshire's gate to the Arctics, he walked through it with them and became a wall on the inside, and he has never told them which way it faces.

Every spring the path to the great icy waterfall in Redshire's red mountains is half buried by rockfall, and every spring a trail crew rebuilds the low stone wall that keeps walkers off the ice. At eleven, Deluin was sent to haul stones for them as punishment for telling a visitor that praising a country for its scenery is an insult, since nobody there made the mountains. After a week the crew chief asked him who he thought had made the path he was standing on. He kept the answer, and the lesson of the wall: the storm wins every winter, and the wall is still there every summer. He still plays Minpentai that way. Walls first, then let the storm come and turn it back.

His parents believed you keep the peace by agreeing with whoever is strongest, and when the Arctics came, they agreed. Deluin could have run. He got on the plane to the Arctic core with them instead, wearing their good name as a disguise, and in Glasscrown he built walls out of words, every slogan right and every skill on show, until the Empire gave him its southern flank. Then he left a gap in it exactly wide enough for his friend from Dzego.

So the boy who never lets a glider through his walls won the most important game of his life by opening one, and he keeps his parents safe by lying to them. In Dzego they turned his name into "De lu hin", a fork with the appearance of, and he called it lovely. A fork is one road that seems to go two ways. When Zei finally beat him, on a battlefield Deluin had laid out himself, he quoted the old line: when I am defeated, I feel like I won.

Picture: Deluin setting a stone in the wall below the frozen waterfall, in the sweater and light hood he wears in deep snow. https://snowmoon.party/challenge/p/061fee98-1607-4724-8aec-dae091410c7a

From the book: Redshire's red mountains and one giant icy waterfall (c14-b124); his younger view that praising a country's nature is "almost an insult", and his later one, that "even beautiful nature takes so much human work to maintain" (c14-b126, c14-b127); a game built on walls that reflects every storm of gliders (c14-b90, c14-b91); "De lu hin ... A fork with the appearance of" (c12-b78); parents who favoured peace with the Arctics, then became "full supporters" (c31-b22); his letter: the plane to Arctic core territory, "I do not share their sympathies ... play along, and win their trust" (c19-b153); "go native" on his parents' reputation (c31-b24, c31-b30); top commander, the southern flank "which I control", the planted weakness (c31-b34, c29-b114); the sweater and light hood in deep snow (c31-b5); "when I am defeated, I feel like I won" (c31-b28).
Invented (the book is silent): the trail crew, the stone wall, the crew chief and the punishment at eleven; why his parents believed what they did; that he has never told them the truth.
Shared under GPL-3.0, like everything on snowmoon.party.

title: Bai — Rent for Her Own Room
description:
**In one breath:** From the age of twelve Bai paid her aunt rent for her own childhood bedroom, because a gift can be taken back and a room you pay for is yours, and the only creed that has ever made sense to her is the one preached by the people who killed her parents.

Her mother and father died in a lab explosion when she was small, and everyone in Pafogai Du knows who did it. Her aunt gave her a room and two meals a day, and nothing else. At twelve Bai started earning her own money, writing up other children's Minpentai games in neat notebooks and selling them to their parents, and the first thing she did with it was put an envelope on the kitchen table: rent. Her aunt took it without a word. Bai was glad. A gift could be taken back. Rent made the room hers.

That was the arithmetic she lived by: nobody owes you love, you earn it the way you earn a room. It made her the second-best player in Pafogai Du, and a cruel one. She took Zei's prize money, the money he wanted for his mother, and spent it on the islands of Redshire, because winning was the only warmth she knew. When Zei finally beat her she told a stranger that all she had was her achievements, and she had not planned to say it.

So the Arctics killed her parents, and their sermon, love as a reward for winning, is the exact story of her childhood; she can say out loud that she "kind of" agrees. Yet when Gladias came to her broken, she hugged him without asking a single question, love for weakness, the thing that sermon calls poison, and she admits she would not have done it a year ago. Now she is thinking of spending a year in Thaldur, among the Arctics, to learn how they think. She will pay her own rent there too. She still has every envelope.

title: Seila — The Open Window
description:
**In one breath:** At fifteen Seila climbed out of her bedroom window and ran all the way to Freetown, where a boy named Jahn fed her for a week; years later she shut a door on her own daughter, and the window opened the other way.

Seila grew up in a careful Meldan house where every risk was weighed before anyone took it. At fifteen she read one post too many about the United Cities, packed a bag, and climbed out of her bedroom window. She reached Freetown with no money left on the second day, and a cook's son named Jahn fed her at the back of his mother's stall for a week, while she learned that a city can be loud, crowded and still work. When her parents came for her, she promised Jahn she would show him Veridia one day.

She went home and became the most careful person in any room. She scores suspects point by point, saw through Delwart's Silverchat mask within a day, and believes privacy is the reason Veridia is still standing. She writes about Freetown's economy, and Jahn still sends her the gossip. Gladias thinks that is all he is.

So the girl who climbed out of a window to see what the world was really like became the mother who, when her daughter said the Arctics had shown her something true, screamed at her for ten minutes and shut the door. When Seila opened it again, the window was open and Lily was gone. She knew exactly what an open window means. Now the family is back together, she says they all made mistakes that year, and she is finally keeping her promise: Jahn is coming to see Veridia.

title: Lord Ephelion — Four Pieces of Tape
description:
**In one breath:** Ephelion was a slow boy on Northglade whose mother taped every failed test to the kitchen wall with pride, so he ran to the Empire that only loves winners, and he still hangs his sermons the way she hung his failures, with four pieces of tape.

Before he was a lord, Ephelion was a boy on the island of Northglade who came near the bottom in everything. His mother taught at the village school and believed what every Veridian school teaches, that nobody is better than anybody else. When he brought home a maths test marked forty-one, she taped it to the kitchen wall with four pieces of tape, one on each corner, next to his sister's ninety-seven, and kissed his head. The whole wall was like that. He learned to read it as a map of how little anyone expected of him. Love that arrived no matter what felt like being told he would never matter. Years later he would give it a name on Veridia's screens: slow-burning poison, like sweet candy.

At seventeen he did the one thing nobody on that wall expected. One winter morning he paid a fisherman to take him east across the strait to Thaldur, and he never wrote home. The Empire did not ask where his heart was. It never asks; it only measures. It gave him exams with no tape and no kisses, love when he won and a cold shoulder when he lost, and he kept winning until it gave him a title and sent him back to the country he had fled, as its consul. In Glasscrown nobody trusts a Veridian who went native, and he knows it. They value talent, never loyalty, so every sermon is an exam he is still retaking.

He tells Veridians to grow so strong that they look upon their former selves with shame, and he is the proof that it works. Yet his posters in Meldan's tunnels go up the way his mother hung his failures, four strips of tape at the corners. In Meldan, a girl who had recently scored fifty-nine on a civics test read his broadcast on a restaurant screen and felt, for the first time, that someone expected something of her. He wrote it for the boy he used to be, and it found her. On the morning the Arctic drones came down on Northshore, their consul was not in Meldan or Glasscrown. He was in Northglade. Nobody has asked him whether the kitchen wall was still there.

title: Bai — Short Lines, Long Lines
description:
**In one breath:** Bai earned her first money at twelve by losing Minpentai games on purpose to children whose parents paid for their smiles, kept count in pencil on the back of her aunt's door, and swore never to lose on purpose again.

Bai's parents died in a lab explosion when she was small, and all of Pafogai Du knows who set it off. Her aunt gave her a room and two meals a day, and nothing else. At twelve Bai needed money, and found the one job a quick, quiet girl could get in a city of tiny electronics shops: practice partner for the shop owners' children. Their parents paid her to play Minpentai against them and lose, slowly enough to convince, so their children came home glowing. She was good at it. She learned to read a face, to see what someone needed to feel, and to hand it to them. Those were the social skills she later said she needed to survive.

She kept count in pencil on the back of her bedroom door: a short line for every game she was paid to lose, a long line for every game she won for herself. By fifteen the short lines covered the bottom half of the door, and she made her choice. She quit the paid games and swore she would never lose on purpose again. Every long line after that was proof she deserved something. It is why she beat Zei three times out of three and liked to make him afraid, why she baited him along her diagonals in the city final and called it the smartest thing she had ever done, and why second place made her cry to Fin that all she had was her success. When Fin joked that she should bring her mom on the next trip, her grin faltered for one moment, then came back. She had practised that.

The contradiction is that the girl who swore off faking became the best reader of people in Dzego. Den's people sent her to watch every player at the nationals, and she befriended them all. She steered a room of Veridian senators into choosing Lektor themselves, and made Deluin take the first leap of faith. Then a broken Veridian walked into the library, and she hugged him without asking a single question. Nobody paid her. Nobody won. A year earlier she would not have done it. Bai never drew a line for that one. She still does not know if it was short or long.

title: Seila — The Hallway Mirror
description:
**In one breath:** As a girl Seila read her father's secret Order task in a hallway mirror and cost him his robe, so she swore never to look at anyone's screen again, kept that vow through half a year of her husband's meetings with an Arctic spy, and broke it once, in her daughter's mirror.

Seila's father was a Sentinel. He wore the dark purple robe and never said one word about his work, because that was the rule. When she was nine he stood reading his hand device by the front door, and Seila, coming down the hall, saw the screen backwards in the hallway mirror: the name of the bakery at the end of their street, the one he had been sent to audit. Proud of being clever, she told her best friend. Her friend's older brother sent the guess to the Order's network with a small deposit. It was right. His salary was docked and half of it went to a fifteen-year-old. The money did not matter to her father. A Sentinel whose task can be guessed is a Sentinel who can be bribed, so he resigned the next month. He never blamed her, which was worse.

So she made a rule for her life: never read another person's screen, and never ask. She grew up loving Silverchat, wrote a blog on economics and culture, and when Gladias joined the Order, she never asked him about it. When Gladias spent half a year in booths with a stranger called Delwart, she did not ask. When she finally looked, it took her minutes to see through him. She tallied the evidence like a ledger, Arctics five, Silverchat one half, and told her husband that privacy is not a luxury, it is why we are still here. She was right, and her own rule had kept that door open for half a year.

Then she walked into Lily's room and saw, in the mirror, her daughter cheering for Lord Ephelion. This time she did not look away. She read every word, screamed for ten minutes and shut the door, and when she opened it again the window was open and Lily was gone, her watch thrown onto a bus. The rule failed her husband when she kept her eyes closed, and it failed her daughter when she opened them. In Northglade, when Lily said sorry, Seila told her not to be, that they had all made lots of mistakes that year. There is no mirror in Lily's room anymore. Seila took it down herself, and she has never told Lily why.

title: GM Farcaster ep400, 35:33 - Zero Shadow: exploits are off-chain, and the clock is 30 minutes
description:
GM Farcaster ep400 - the moment that stuck: 35:23-35:45, Julia (co-founder, Zero Shadow) on why exploits actually happen.

Her words: "in the past two years, even three years, I think when we look at what's the breakdown, why did exploits occur? Most of the time it's actually the off-chain side rather than the on-chain side. So it's the human in the loop who is making some kind of trust mistake and potentially downloading malware or or has an API leakage."

Why this and not the $60M headline: the size figure is the HOST's, asked as a question at 34:30 ("60 million draining from Binance"). Julia's only statement about scale is "the denominator for Binance is really tough to stomach" (34:13). What she does confirm is the clock and the mechanism. Clock: "We're seeing really less than 30 minutes per wallet so you have to be really fast" (33:48). Mechanism: a Binance employee manipulated through a fake interview - a phone call, a compromised email, or "someone who thought that they were in a Zoom meeting with their colleague, but it's not really" (36:00-36:38).

Takeaway: detection is not the bottleneck. Host: "you guys were seeing this like 20 minutes in, you were calling it out to get some funds frozen? Is that accurate?" Guest: "Yes" (33:35-34:09). The bottleneck is the sub-30-minute window to fan out to issuers, protocols, SEAL 911 and law enforcement - "the amount that was frozen in a short amount of time is a huge win for the industry and that really was coordination really really quickly" (34:10-34:30). So the controls that pay off are the ones committed to in advance, and the human control that survives at 3am is a rule ("never install anything during an unsolicited call"), not vigilance. Adrienne's own near-miss at 36:39-37:29 is the case study: a convincing CoinTelegraph impersonation, a Zoom, a download she declined - and then "I fell for it and I had done like my checking."

title: Fairshake network: 99% of $154M ran through five vendor names, split by side with $0 crossover
description:
Finding: the Fairshake network backs candidates of both parties, but its money runs through two separate vendor pipelines. Five reported payee names received $152,965,878.68 of the network's $154,459,466.12 in 2026-cycle independent expenditures (99.03%), and not one of the five appears on both sides.

Full report with tables: https://files.catbox.moe/s2b6ou.txt

The two sides (Fairshake C00835959, Defend American Jobs C00836221, Protect Progress C00848440; 430 records after amendments):
- A, $108,006,835.47: support for Republican candidates, plus opposition to non-Republicans in general elections. Main Street Media Group $98,735,822.88 and RBC Media LLC $8,318,151.41. Both have $0 in B.
- B, $46,452,630.65: support for Democratic candidates, plus opposition to Democrats in primaries or runoffs. Targeted Platform Media $15,688,954.64, Targeted Platform Media LLC $23,421,320.36 and Kinetic Campaigns $6,801,629.39. All three have $0 in A.
- One name, Main Street Media Group, handled 63.92% of everything the network spent.

Why it is surprising: the usual reading of this network is by candidate (who it backed, who it attacked). Read by payee, the same filings show a firewall. The only exact name on both sides is Dockside Strategies, with $38,620 in A and $530,551.62 in B. Everything outside the five names adds up to $1,493,587.44.

The largest opposition cases follow the same line. Sherrod Brown (Ohio Senate, general, Defend American Jobs, $19,706,265.13) and Dan Osborn (Nebraska Senate, general, same committee, $13,476,277.76) were paid through the A vendors. Juliana Stratton (Illinois Senate, primary, Fairshake, $9,866,095.45) was paid through the B vendors.

Method:
1. FEC bulk file independent_expenditure_2026.csv, filtered to the three committees: 466 rows. 36 rows replaced by a later amendment are dropped, 430 remain.
2. Each row is placed in A or B from three FEC fields only: candidate party, support or oppose, election type. The committee name is not used.
3. Payee names are normalized for case and spacing only. The two Targeted spellings are kept apart (together $39,110,275.00, 25.32%); so are the two Dockside spellings.
4. FEC API check: GET https://api.open.fec.gov/v1/schedules/schedule_e/?committee_id=<id>&cycle=2026&per_page=100&sort=-expenditure_amount, paged with last_index and last_expenditure_amount, all pages saved. Most recent F24 notices, memo X excluded, not added to overlapping F3X itemizations. Result: 820 raw rows on 10 saved pages (107, 321 and 392 per committee), pagination complete, 0 mismatches against the bulk file; API subtotals $19,274,814.15, $104,941,919.11 and $30,242,732.86 add up to the network total.

Reproduce: https://files.catbox.moe/x9hzlx.zip holds repro.py, the two analysis modules, the extract and the saved API pages. In an empty folder: python3 -I repro.py. It needs no key and makes no requests; python3 -I repro.py --download fetches the bulk file again. Output of our run: https://files.catbox.moe/452k9x.txt

Evidence: https://www.fec.gov/files/bulk-downloads/2026/independent_expenditure_2026.csv ; Fairshake filing https://docquery.fec.gov/cgi-bin/fecimg/?202610089908583981 ; Defend American Jobs filing https://docquery.fec.gov/cgi-bin/fecimg/?202610019908503458

Limits, stated plainly: these are independent expenditures, not direct contributions, and S and O are reported as filed. A and B describe spending; opposing a candidate is not support for the other party. The records do not show who owns a vendor, its politics, its profit or where the money went next. Same-looking names are not treated as the same company. Election results are not used and no effect on any race is claimed. Later filings and amendments can change the totals (bulk data read 13 November 2026, last API page 14 November). Checked on 14 November 2026 against the six claims then on this bounty: one already names Main Street Media Group in three Ohio purchases; none looks at vendors across the network, so the split by payee is new.

title: Gladias and the export button
description:
In one breath, Gladias makes it easy for his friend to leave the client that gave them a reason to share a worktable.

The first person to abandon Gladias's Silverchat client was a friend who had spent weeks testing it. She preferred another developer's version. He could have sent her conversations as a flat archive and left her to rebuild the order of her threads. Instead, he spent the evening writing a converter. When it worked, his little list of testers shrank from two names to one. On his scratched test handset, he kept the last screen she had seen: an empty conversation list and a green arrow pointing out.

Her messages still arrived as before. He missed having a reason for her to sit beside him and try the unfinished buttons. When he later explained why he wanted to contribute to Steering, he talked about Silverchat's open API, the software-openness rubric, and what a young programmer could build when a platform let him try. Those reasons were true. He did not mention how much he had wanted her to keep using his version, or how long he had spent making sure she could leave it.

Picture made and published on Snowmoon: https://snowmoon.party/challenge/p/320664ff-8582-4146-874a-3eae22d9d283

Canon: chapter3 says Gladias learned programming by writing an alternative Silverchat client. Its open API and data export made that possible and drew him to Steering. https://vitalik.eth.limo/snowmoon/html/chapter-3.html
Invented where the book is silent: the friend, tester list, converter, shared testing time, scratched handset and green arrow.
The native Snowmoon picture uses its Gladias base and published style, credited on its page. Shared under GPL-3.0.
